why_this_tool: MLflow is open source, runs fully on a laptop, and exposes the same client API, backend store and artifact store split that a platform engineer has to operate in production.
alternatives: Weights and Biases is a hosted tracker with richer dashboards but a paid tier, Neptune and Comet are similar hosted services, ClearML and Aim are open-source and self-hosted like MLflow (ClearML adds orchestration, Aim focuses on fast run comparison), TensorBoard only visualises metrics and has no registry, and DVC tracks experiments in Git instead of on a server.

setup.do: Create a fresh Python virtual environment and install MLflow into it with pip.
setup.done_when: Running the mlflow command with the version flag prints a version number.

source.title: Tracking Experiments with Local Database | MLflow AI Platform

setup.why: A clean environment keeps the MLflow version pinned and separate from other projects. Every later step uses this one install for the client, the UI and the server.

setup.do: Point MLflow at a local SQLite database by setting the tracking URI as the tutorial shows.
setup.done_when: A SQLite database file appears in your working directory after the first logged run.

verified.section_found: Step 3 - Train a model with MLflow Autologging

steps.why: This is the shortest route to a real run. It shows what MLflow captures without any logging code.

steps.do: Write a second script that creates a named experiment, starts a run and logs params, metrics, tags and one artifact file explicitly.
steps.done_when: The new experiment shows a run whose params, metrics and artifact match exactly what your script logged.

source.title: MLflow Tracking APIs | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: Explicit logging makes the data model concrete: experiments hold runs, and runs hold params, metrics, tags and artifacts. You need it whenever autologging does not cover a library.

steps.do: Start a tracking server with an explicit relational backend store URI and log a run to it.
steps.done_when: The server starts against your database, and the run is still listed after you restart the server.
steps.why: The backend store holds run metadata such as params, metrics and tags. Choosing and configuring it is the first decision when operating the server.

steps.do: Configure a separate artifact store location for the server and log a model file to it.
steps.done_when: The artifact files appear under the location you configured, and the run page shows that artifact URI.
steps.why: Artifacts are stored apart from metadata because they are large files. Seeing the two stores side by side explains the server architecture.

steps.do: Configure autologging for one library only, change its options such as model logging, and combine it with one explicit metric.
steps.done_when: A new run contains the autologged values plus your explicit metric, and the option you turned off is absent.

source.title: Automatic Logging with MLflow Tracking | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: A platform team makes autologging the default but must control what it records. Mixing it with explicit calls is the usual pattern in real training code.

steps.do: Run the training script several times with different hyperparameters, then query the runs programmatically with a filter and an ordering on one metric.
steps.done_when: The query returns a table of runs sorted by your metric, and the top row matches the best run shown in the UI.

source.title: ML Experiment Tracking | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: Comparison is the purpose of tracking. A programmatic query is what automation uses to pick the best run.

steps.do: Register the model from the best run in the Model Registry with the Python API.
steps.done_when: The Models page shows your registered model at version 1 with a link back to the source run.

source.title: ML Model Registry | MLflow AI Platform

verified.section_found: Register a model with MLflow Python APIs

steps.why: Registration turns a run artifact into a named, versioned model. That version can be traced back to the run that produced it.

steps.do: Read the deployment section of the ML overview and note which local serving options exist for a registered model.
steps.done_when: You can name the local serving route you would use for your registered model and which guide covers it.

source.title: MLflow AI Engineering Platform | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: Tracking feeds serving, so you should know where a tracked model goes next. This page is the entry point to the serving guides.

steps.do: Log the training dataset as a tracked input of a run, with its source and digest.
steps.done_when: The run page shows the dataset name, digest and source next to its params and metrics.

source.title: ML Dataset Tracking | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: A result is reproducible only when the run records the data as well as the code and params. Dataset tracking stores that lineage on the run.

steps.do: Enable system metrics logging through the environment variable and rerun the training script without changing its code.
steps.done_when: The run shows a system metrics section with CPU and memory charts although the script was not edited.

verified.section_found: Using the Environment Variable to Control System Metrics Logging

steps.why: Environment variables are how a platform makes logging the default for every job and CI run. System metrics also record the resource context of each run.

steps.do: Create the compose file from the remote tracking tutorial that defines PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible MinIO store, and start the containers.
steps.done_when: Both containers report as running, and a bucket for artifacts exists in the MinIO console.

source.title: Remote Experiment Tracking with MLflow Tracking Server | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: This is a local substitute for a managed database and cloud object storage. It gives the same backend and artifact store split as production.

steps.do: Launch the tracking server against the PostgreSQL backend and the MinIO artifact store, then log a run to it from a separate client shell.
steps.done_when: A run logged from the client appears in the server UI, with metadata in PostgreSQL and artifact files in the MinIO bucket.

source.title: Remote Experiment Tracking with MLflow Tracking Server | MLflow AI Platform

steps.why: A shared server that proxies artifacts and keeps metadata in a real database is the setup a team relies on. Logging from a separate client proves the full path works.
